reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID (Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease)
clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive defect of the mitochondrial enzyme (ACAT1 gene) that acts in both ketone-body utilisation and isoleucine catabolism, so the disorder combines a ketolysis defect with an organic aciduria

Typically presents in infancy or early childhood with intermittent ketoacidotic crises precipitated by intercurrent infection, fasting, or a high-protein load, often with normal health between episodes
Urine organic acids classically show 2-methyl-3-hydroxybutyrate, 2-methylacetoacetate and tiglylglycine, reflecting the block in isoleucine breakdown
Blood acylcarnitine profile characteristically shows raised C5:1 (tiglylcarnitine) and C5-OH (2-methyl-3-hydroxybutyrylcarnitine)
Severe ketoacidosis during crises can be striking, but unlike SCOT deficiency the ketosis is episodic rather than permanent

Acute management centres on reversing catabolism with intravenous glucose and correcting acidosis; long-term care uses avoidance of prolonged fasting and modest protein moderation with an emergency regimen for illness
Neurological outcome is variable and basal ganglia injury has been reported after severe crises, so prompt treatment of acidotic episodes is important
reference.pathophysiology: Beta-ketothiolase deficiency results from loss of mitochondrial acetoacetyl-CoA thiolase (T2), encoded by ACAT1. The enzyme participates both in the terminal step of ketone-body metabolism and in the catabolism of isoleucine at the level of 2-methylacetoacetyl-CoA. Its deficiency impairs ketone-body handling and blocks isoleucine degradation, so intermediates such as 2-methyl-3-hydroxybutyrate, 2-methylacetoacetate and tiglylglycine accumulate. During catabolic stress, when fatty-acid oxidation and ketogenesis are upregulated, the inability to process ketoacids leads to profound ketoacidosis. Episodes are typically intermittent, with metabolic decompensation triggered by fasting, infection, or protein loading.
additionalDifferentials: Maple syrup urine disease during decompensation
Salicylate or other toxic ingestion causing anion-gap acidosis
Glycogen storage disease with ketotic hypoglycaemia
additionalInvestigations: Urine organic acid analysis for 2-methyl-3-hydroxybutyrate, 2-methylacetoacetate and tiglylglycine
Plasma acylcarnitine profile by tandem mass spectrometry looking for raised C5:1 and C5-OH
Blood gas, glucose, electrolytes and calculated anion gap during acute presentations
Blood and urine ketone quantification to document ketoacidosis
Molecular genetic testing of ACAT1 to confirm the diagnosis
Enzyme assay or in-vitro loading studies in fibroblasts where genetics are inconclusive
redFlags: Severe high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis with heavy ketosis in an unwell child
Reduced consciousness or seizures suggesting cerebral involvement during a crisis
Recurrent unexplained ketoacidotic episodes triggered by illness or fasting
Haemodynamic instability from profound dehydration and acidosis
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is generally favourable when crises are recognised and treated promptly, and many individuals develop normally with few episodes after childhood. However, severe or poorly managed ketoacidotic crises can cause basal ganglia injury and lasting neurological sequelae.
pitfalls: Attributing severe ketoacidosis to presumed diabetes or gastroenteritis and missing the underlying metabolic disorder
Assuming a normal interictal examination excludes a serious inherited condition
Failing to send urine organic acids and acylcarnitines during the acute episode when abnormalities are most informative
Under-treating catabolism by not providing adequate intravenous glucose during illness
references: Scriver's OMMBID: Disorders of Ketone Body Metabolism
Saudubray, Baumgartner & Walter, Inborn Metabolic Diseases: Diagnosis and Treatment
management: Treat acute ketoacidotic crises with intravenous glucose to reverse catabolism, correcting acidosis with fluids and electrolytes
Prevent decompensation by avoiding prolonged fasting and providing an emergency regimen with glucose-containing feeds during intercurrent illness
Institute modest dietary protein moderation to reduce isoleucine loading while maintaining adequate growth
Consider carnitine supplementation to support removal of accumulated acyl intermediates
Educate the family on sick-day rules and early presentation with a written emergency protocol
Monitor growth, development and metabolic control with a metabolic dietitian, surveilling for basal ganglia injury after severe crises
Confirm with ACAT1 testing and offer genetic counselling and family screening for this autosomal recessive disorder
